# The permutations generated by Hamilton viewpoints

**PROVED.** Let a Hamilton word of a finite tournament be an ordering of all vertices with an arc from each letter to its successor. For two Hamilton words of the same tournament put
\[
 f_{P,Q}(p_i)=q_i,\qquad G(T)=\langle f_{P,Q}: P,Q\text{ Hamilton words}\rangle .
\]
The group splits as the direct product of the groups on the strongly connected components (SCCs), acting on their own vertices. On a nonsingleton strong tournament of order \(n\),
\[
 G(T)=
 \begin{cases}
 A_n & T=C_3\text{ or } T=Q_5=C_3[C_3,K_1,K_1],\\
 S_n & \text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The notation for \(Q_5\) means that one vertex of a directed triangle is replaced by another directed triangle. The singleton has trivial group. In particular the orbits of \(G(T)\) recover the SCC partition.

Fixing any one source word \(P\) gives the same generated group, since \(f_{Q,R}=f_{P,R}f_{P,Q}^{-1}\). To read off the actual class fiber at that source, retain just the permutations \(g\) satisfying \(g(p_i)\to g(p_{i+1})\) at every position. Reading the remaining arcs in that order gives its board. Two accepted words give the same board exactly when the coordinate-wise map between them is an automorphism. This yields \(H(T)/|\operatorname{Aut}T|\) distinct boards. Given any input board at any size, the lexicographically least board obtained by these accepted words is an ordinary class key; taking the minimum of this key and the key of its staircase reflection gives a merged class key. This is an exact quotient map, with potentially factorial cost. The sign of a relative permutation is a different binary observable from a line's blue or black color. [THM-796, tiling/line/node incidence](../../../01-canon/theorems/THM-796-three-sorted-recursive-tiling-line-node-incidence.md)

## Rotating a cycle with one vertex exposed

Every Hamilton word concatenates words of the SCCs in their unique forward order. Conversely every such concatenation works, and one can vary each factor independently. This proves the product assertion.

Suppose \(T\) is strong, \(n\ge4\). Take a directed cycle \(C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})\) on \(m=n-1\) vertices. Such a cycle exists by Moon's theorem. The omitted vertex \(w\) beats some but not all of \(C\). Let \(\gamma=(c_0\ c_1\ \cdots\ c_{m-1})\) fix \(w\). For any two outneighbors of \(w\) at positions \(i,j\), prepend \(w\) to the cuts of \(C\) starting there. Comparing these Hamilton words gives \(\gamma^{j-i}\in G\). Using cuts ending at two inneighbors and appending \(w\) gives the same assertion for the other color. Let \(d\) be the gcd of \(m\) and all these within-color differences. Each color lies in one residue class modulo \(d\), and together they cover all the positions. Thus \(d\le2\) and \(\gamma^d\in G\). The case \(d=2\) is exactly an alternating cycle of even length. [Moon, *On subtournaments of a tournament*](https://doi.org/10.4153/CMB-1966-038-7)

Rotate the subscripts so that \(c_{m-1}\to w\to c_0\). Cutting the resulting Hamilton cycle at two successive positions gives \(\eta=(c_0\ \cdots\ c_{m-1}\ w)\in G\). For \(d=1\), the product \(\eta\gamma^{-1}\) transposes the consecutive vertices \(w,c_0\); conjugation by \(\eta\) supplies all consecutive transpositions. For \(d=2\), the product \(\eta^2\gamma^{-2}\) cycles the three consecutive vertices \(w,c_0,c_1\). Its rotations generate \(A_n\). Indeed the consecutive transpositions generate \(S_n\), and each product of two of them factors into products of neighboring transpositions in pairs by telescoping along the interval between them. Each neighboring pair is a consecutive 3-cycle or its inverse. Thus \(G\supseteq A_n\), and already \(G=S_n\) whenever \(n\) is even or the contacts fail to alternate. For a triangle the three cuts themselves give \(A_3\).

## A seven-vertex obstruction to one permutation sign

It remains to handle odd \(n\) with alternating contacts. Assume \(n\ge7\) and all Hamilton words have the same permutation sign. Choose six consecutive vertices of \(C\), locally numbered \(0,1,\ldots,5\), with \(0,2,4\to w\to1,3,5\), and write \(6=w\). The word \((0,6,1,2,3,4,5)\) has odd sign in these local labels. Any even local Hamilton word **starting at 0 or ending at 5** contradicts the assumption. For a word starting at 0 prepend the rest of the cycle immediately before 0 in its forward order; for one ending at 5 append the rest after 5. The displayed odd word allows either extension, so the relative sign survives.

Here is the complete finite lemma used on this window. Number the ten free chords \((i,j)\) for \(0\le i<j-1\le4\) in lexicographic order, starting at bit zero; a one orients the chord forwards. Among the 1,024 masks, exactly \(855,863,967,975\) have no even Hamilton word with the indicated endpoint condition. In all four masks \(0\to2\) and \(3\to5\). To reproduce the lemma, start each possible word at each of the seven vertices, repeatedly extend by an unused outneighbor, and at length seven test the sign and the endpoint disjunction. The standalone certificate gives the masks and their forced bits. [Finite certificate](viewpoints.py)

Advance the window by two positions at a time. The first forced chord makes every even-start distance-two chord forward, and the last makes every odd-start distance-two chord forward, with indices cyclically modulo \(m\). Now the even word \((0,2,4,6,1,3,5)\) connects both ends of any such window. This is a contradiction. In the remaining order five, the same script enumerates all \(2^6\) boards containing the marked ascending path. Of the six strong classes only one has a single sign. Its height is 15 and its number of boards is five. The rows \((16,5,9,3,14)\) describe \(Q_5\); the three internal cyclic orders each give five cuts, all of the same sign. Its internal triangle is necessarily contiguous around a Hamilton cycle, and exhaustive enumeration on these five rows gives the same fifteen full paths. This identifies the exceptional class. A separate proof using cut vertices and a quantitative minority-sign inequality is in [SECOND-PROOF.md](SECOND-PROOF.md).

## What the group loses

The cut words of one Hamilton cycle generate just its cyclic rotation group. Even adjoining all path words and generating \(S_n\) loses most of the path constraints. Pair positions \((1,2),(3,4),\ldots\) in every proposed ordering. Of the \(2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) arrangements obtained by independently switching each of those pairs, at most one has the required arcs inside all pairs. Hence \(H(T)/n!\le 2^{-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\). With a reference \(P\), the set of actual maps \(f_{P,Q}\) is itself a group precisely when every SCC is a singleton or triangle. On these components every cyclic rotation works, independently. Every other component has an even-order generated group (including \(A_5\)), whereas the actual set has odd cardinality by Rédei. Distinct geometric path words can thus compose to an ordering which violates a backbone arc. The [Hamilton-path relocation graph](../hamilton_path_relocation_connectivity_20261020/THEOREM.txt) retains physical intermediate words for its different, local operation.

For a self-converse class the staircase reflection preserves the two permutation-sign fibers individually, relative to any fixed reference. Indeed any automorphism is even: the automorphism group has odd order since an involution cannot preserve the arc between a swapped pair. Choose an involution reversing the tournament (Cauchy's theorem on the automorphism/anti-automorphism group, with the singleton immediate). It fixes at most one vertex and therefore has the sign of the reversal of the positions. To reflect a word inside the same class one both reverses its order and applies that involution. Their signs cancel. On each of the two sign fibers the number of blue boards consequently has the parity of the size of that fiber. These statements concern board colors under reflection; classification by permutation parity is independent of any coloring convention.
